This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $A$ be a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that all pairwise distances are at least $1$ and if two distinct distances differ then they differ by at least $1$. Is the diameter of $A$ $\gg n$?
#100: [Er90][Er92e][Er95][Er97f]
geometry | 
distances
Perhaps the diameter is even $\geq n-1$ for sufficiently large $n$. Piepmeyer has an example of $9$ such points with diameter $<5$. Kanold proved the diameter is $\geq n^{3/4}$. The bounds on the distinct distance problem [89] proved by Guth and Katz [GuKa15] imply a lower bound of $\gg n/\log n$.
Additional thanks to: Shengtong Zhang, Boris Alexeev, and Dustin Mixon

 In [Er95], in the same passage that describes Piepmeyer's example, Erdős adds: "It is perhaps not uninteresting to try to determine the smallest diameter for each $n$, but this will already be difficult for $n=9$." That case can be settled, and Piepmeyer's example turns out to be optimal.
Write $\delta(n)$ for the smallest possible diameter. The hypothesis is scale-dependent and the conclusion is not, so normalise: for a set $X$ with distinct distances $d_1<\cdots<d_k$, put $g=\min(d_1,\min_i(d_{i+1}-d_i))$, so the least diameter the shape of $X$ permits is $\delta(X)=d_k/g$. Since $d_k\ge d_1+(k-1)g\ge kg$, we get $\delta(X)\ge k$, the number of distinct distances; this is eq. (8) of Kanold, Abh. Braunschw. Wiss. Ges. 32 (1981) 55-65. So a configuration can only improve on an incumbent value $D$ if it has fewer than $D$ distinct distances. Piepmeyer's set gives $4.664<5$, hence at $n=7,8,9$ only sets with at most four distances compete, and those are classified: Erdős and Fishburn (Discrete Math. 160 (1996) 115-125, Thm. 1) for nine points, Shinohara (Discrete Math. 308 (2008) 3048-3055, Thm. 1.2) for eight, Lan and Wei (Mat. Zametki 93 (2013) 492-508, Thm. 8) for seven, together with the three-distance sets of Shinohara (European J. Combin. 25 (2004) 1039-1058). Evaluating $d_k/g$ over those lists gives
$$\delta(7)=\delta(8)=\delta(9)=\frac{2+\sqrt3}{1+\sqrt3-\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}}=\sqrt{6+3\sqrt3+4\sqrt2+2\sqrt6}=4.663902460\ldots,$$
attained only by Piepmeyer's configuration and its subsets. In particular the page's "diameter $<5$" is sharp at $n=9$.
Piepmeyer's nine points are the configuration Erdős and Fishburn describe as "three equilateral triangles with the same center", which they single out as the only realizer of any $g(k)$ that is neither a regular polygon (with or without its centre) nor a subset of the triangular lattice. Their paper does not mention Piepmeyer.
For $n\le6$, deciding every colouring of the pairs by distance class with a Gröbner basis and listing all real solutions gives $\delta(3)=1$, $\delta(4)=(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)/(\sqrt6+\sqrt2-2)=2.073132\ldots$, $\delta(5)=(3+\sqrt5)/2$, $\delta(6)=2+\sqrt2$. For $n=10,11,12$ the same argument gives $\delta(n)\ge6$, with $\delta(10)\le8.290859\ldots$ (the regular nonagon plus its centre) and $\delta(11),\delta(12)\le6+3\sqrt3$ (subsets of the triangular lattice); I do not know whether these are sharp. One caveat: the floor $6$ at $n=10$ uses my own reading of the single configuration in Wei's classification of 10-point 5-distance sets (Electron. J. Combin. 19 (2012) #P38, Thm. 11) that appears there only as a figure, namely the regular pentagon together with the five intersection points of its diagonals; without that reading the floor is $5$.

 Three remarks on the sources for this problem from tracking down its history.
It appeared as Erdős, Problem 856A, Elem. Math. 36 (1981) 22, solved by Kanold in Elem. Math. 37 (1982) 56. I have not seen those two pages; I know of them from Kanold's own 1981 paper, which quotes the problem and restates his published solution, diameter $>(\varepsilon/4)n^{3/4}$ for $n\ge16$.
The page says Kanold proved the diameter is $\ge n^{3/4}$. In the plane his paper (Über Punktmengen im $k$-dimensionalen euklidischen Raum, Abh. Braunschw. Wiss. Ges. 32 (1981) 55-65) proves more. Write $d$ for the smallest distance in the set and $\varepsilon$ for the smallest difference between two distinct distances. His Satz 2 has two cases: if $d\le\varepsilon$ then $\mathrm{diam}/\varepsilon>n/2$, and only when $d>\varepsilon$ does one fall back to $\mathrm{diam}/\varepsilon>0.366\,n^{3/4}$. So the linear bound this problem asks for is already proved whenever the smallest distance does not exceed the smallest gap, and the whole difficulty sits in the opposite regime. Piepmeyer's example lies there: its distances are $1.2496\ldots,\ 1+\sqrt2,\ 2+\sqrt2,\ 4.6639\ldots$, so the smallest gap is exactly $1$ while the smallest distance is larger.
Finally, P. Brass, "On the Erdős-diameter of sets", Discrete Math. 150 (1996) 415-419, is a paper devoted to exactly this quantity: it names the minimum diameter $\delta(n)$ and proves an asymptotic form of Erdős's conjecture $\delta(n)=n-1$ for sets contained in a parallel half-strip. It seems worth citing here. I have only been able to see its abstract, so I cannot say what else it contains.
